units:
Introduction and Mathematical Foundations
Q1. Discuss the major goals of AI—perception, reasoning, planning, communication, creativity,
learning, and control/manipulation—and explain how Generative AI is contributing to these
goals.
Q2. Explain the major capabilities of Generative AI with its major applications. Explain how the
scaling of Generative AI models depends on data, model parameters, computational resources,
memory, and distributed training. Discuss why scaling becomes increasingly challenging as
model size increases.
Q3. Differentiate between discriminative and generative models in terms of the probability
distributions they learn, their objectives, and their applications. Explain how a generative model
can also perform a discriminative task using the relationship between joint and conditional
probability distributions.
Q4. Explain the major challenges in deep generative modeling, particularly for high-dimensional
data such as images. Explain how these challenges affect the ability to generate realistic
samples and perform discriminative tasks.
Q5. Explain the fundamental rules of probability, including joint probability, conditional
probability, the sum rule, and the product rule. Derive Bayes’ theorem from the product rule and
explain the roles of prior, likelihood, posterior, and normalization constant.
Q6. Explain the Gaussian distribution and its importance in probability theory. For a dataset of
independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) observations, explain how Maximum Likelihood
Estimation (MLE) can be used to estimate the mean and variance of a Gaussian distribution.
Q7. Explain the fundamental concepts of information theory. Define self-information, Shannon
entropy, KL divergence, and cross-entropy. Discuss the properties of KL divergence and explain
the relationship between cross-entropy and KL divergence.
Q8. Consider a medical diagnosis problem in which an X-ray image of a patient is analyzed to
determine whether the patient has cancer (C₁) or no cancer (C₂). The following information is
available:
Class Prior Probability Likelihood of X-ray Result
Cancer (C₁) 0.10 0.80
No Cancer (C₂) 0.90 0.20
Using Bayes’ theorem, calculate the posterior probability of each class given the observed X-ray
result. Based on the posterior probabilities, determine the appropriate classification decision.
Explain the roles of prior probability, likelihood, posterior probability, and normalization constant
in the decision-making process.

(X∣Y). Explain their objectives with suitable examples.

Determine the predicted class and calculate the negative log-likelihood loss if the actual class is

Q2. Discuss the importance of sampling, interpolation, and disentanglement in exploring the
learned manifold of a deep generative model. Illustrate each concept with a suitable example.
Q3. Compare GANs, VAEs, and Denoising Diffusion Models in terms of their architecture,
training mechanism, sampling process, and ability to generate new data.
Q4. Explain the architecture and working of a Variational Autoencoder (VAE). Discuss how the
encoder predicts the mean and covariance of a multivariate normal distribution, how the
decoder reconstructs the input, and why the latent distribution is encouraged to follow N(0,I).
Q5. Explain why direct sampling from N(μ(X),Σ(X)) creates a problem during backpropagation in
a VAE. Explain the reparameterization trick and show how it enables gradient-based training.
Q6. Consider a one-dimensional latent variable with
μ=2,σ=0.5,ϵ=−1.2,
where ϵ∼N(0,1). Using
z=μ+σϵ,
calculate the latent variable z. If the decoder maps this value according to x′=3z+1, calculate the
generated output x′.
MLE and Latent Variable Model
Q1. Explain the motivation for using latent variable models in deep generative modeling.
Consider an image dataset in which factors such as gender, eye color, hair color, and pose are
not explicitly annotated.
(a) Distinguish between observed variables x and latent variables z.
(b) Explain how latent variables can represent high-level factors of variation.
(c) Describe the generative model p(x∣z) and explain why it may be simpler than directly
Class Probability
Cat 0.10
Dog 0.75
Bird 0.15

modeling p(x).
(d) Discuss how p(z∣x) can be used for unsupervised representation learning.
Q2. For a latent variable model, the log-likelihood is
(a) Explain why Jensen's inequality is applicable to this expression.
(b) Introduce an arbitrary probability distribution q(z) and rewrite the marginal likelihood in terms
of q(z).
(c) Apply Jensen's inequality to derive the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO).
(d) Explain why the resulting quantity is called a lower bound on the log-likelihood.
Q3. For a variational distribution q(z), the relationship between log-likelihood, ELBO, and KL
divergence is
(a) Explain why DKL(q∥p)≥0 implies that ELBO is a lower bound.
(b) Derive the above relationship between log-likelihood, ELBO, and KL divergence.
(c) State the condition under which the ELBO becomes equal to the true log-likelihood.
(d) Explain what happens to the ELBO as q(z;ϕ) becomes a better approximation to the true
posterior.
Q4. Suppose a latent variable z has 4 possible configurations and the joint probabilities for a
given observation x are:
(a) Calculate the marginal likelihood p(x).
(b) Calculate p(zi∣x) for each latent configuration.
(c) Identify the most probable latent configuration based on the posterior.
(d) Explain how this posterior inference can be interpreted in the context of clustering or
representation learning.
Generative Adversarial Network
Q1. Explain the architecture and working principle of a Generative Adversarial Network
(GAN). Describe the roles of the generator Gθ and discriminator Dϕ and explain how they
participate in the two-player minimax game. Formulate the GAN objective function and explain
the purpose of each term.
Q2. During discriminator training, suppose the discriminator outputs:
● D(x)=0.9 for a real sample

● D(G(z))=0.2D(G(z))=0.2 for a generated sample.
Using the binary cross-entropy discriminator loss,
LD=−[logD(x)+log(1−D(G(z)))]
calculate LD. Interpret the result.
Q3. Consider for a particular minibatch, suppose the discriminator outputs the following
probabilities:
Sample Type D(x)
x1 Real 0.9
x2 Real 0.8
G(z1) Fake 0.2
G(z2) Fake 0.1
Using
calculate the discriminator objective value V(G,D) using natural logarithms. Determine
whether the discriminator is performing well based on its outputs.
Q4. During one GAN training iteration, the generator produces four fake samples. The
discriminator outputs are
D(G(z1))=0.1,D(G(z2))=0.3,D(G(z3))=0.7,D(G(z4))=0.5.
Using the generator objective given in the lecture,
(a) Calculate the generator loss.
(b) Explain what the magnitude of the loss indicates about the discriminator's ability to
distinguish the generated samples.
(c) If the discriminator outputs become
[0.6,0.7,0.8,0.9],
calculate the new generator loss and compare the two cases.
Q5. Discuss the major practical challenges associated with training GANs. Explain unstable
optimization and mode collapse with suitable examples. In your answer, describe why generator
and discriminator losses may oscillate during training and explain how mode collapse affects the
diversity of generated samples. Also discuss the empirical approaches used to mitigate mode
collapse.

Q6. Consider a GAN with an optimal discriminator DG∗
. Show that the value function can be
expressed in terms of the Jensen–Shannon Divergence (JSD) between pdata and pG:
Define JSD and explain its important properties. What is the condition on pG at the optimum of
the GAN objective, and what is the corresponding value of the objective function?
Q7. Explain why evaluating generative models is challenging. Discuss how the evaluation
strategy depends on the intended task. Explain the evaluation requirements for:
1. Density estimation
2. Sampling/generation
3. Latent representation learning
4. Downstream applications such as semi-supervised learning and image translation.
Q8. Explain the Inception Score (IS) used for evaluating the quality of generated samples.
Discuss why a good generative model should simultaneously exhibit high sharpness and high
diversity, relating to the classifier's predictive distribution c(y∣x) and marginal distribution c(y)
Q9. Explain the Frechet Inception Distance (FID) and its role in evaluating generative models.
Suppose the feature representations of generated samples and test samples are modeled as
multivariate Gaussians with parameters (μG,ΣG) and (μT,ΣT), respectively. Write the FID
formulation as:
Explain each term and describe the interpretation of a low FID value. Also explain how FID
differs conceptually from the Inception Score.
Variants of GAN
1. Explain the architecture and working principle of a Conditional GAN (cGAN). How does
conditioning on class information modify the conventional GAN framework? Explain how cGANs
can be used for text-to-image synthesis.
2. Explain the motivation behind BiGAN (Bidirectional GAN). Describe how the generator G
and encoder E learn the joint distributions of (X,Z), and explain the condition under which E and
G become approximately inverse mappings.
3. Consider two semantically related image domains XAX_A and XBX_B, for which
corresponding image pairs are not available.
(a) Explain how CoGAN (Coupled Generative Adversarial Networks) learns the joint
distribution of the two domains without correspondence supervision.

(b) Explain the role of weight sharing in CoGAN. Why are different layers shared between the
two networks, and how does this model inductive bias help in learning common high-level
semantics? Also discuss one important limitation of CoGAN.
4. Two image domains A and B contain unpaired training images, and the mapping between
the domains is unknown.
(a) Explain the architecture and working principle of CycleGAN for unpaired image-to-image
translation. Define the two mappings GA→B and GB→A, and explain how adversarial loss is used.
(b) Explain the importance of cycle-consistency loss and identity loss in CycleGAN. Discuss
why cycle consistency is necessary and describe a limitation of relying only on
cycle-consistency loss.
5. Explain linear interpolation in the latent space of a GAN. Given two latent vectors z1 and z2
,
derive the interpolated latent vector for a step size α∈[0,1], and explain how the generator
produces the corresponding sequence of images. Explain the concept of steerability of GANs.
How can transformations such as zooming, shifting, brightness adjustment, and rotation in
image space be represented as transformations in latent space?
Q6. Explain the motivation for introducing Bidirectional Generative Adversarial Networks
(BiGANs). Compare BiGAN with a conventional GAN in terms of latent-variable inference.
Describe the roles of the generator G, encoder E, and discriminator D. Explain how the
discriminator distinguishes between the joint samples
(z,G(z))
and
(E(x),x).
How can a trained BiGAN be used both for generating new samples and inferring latent
representations?
Q7. Explain the problem of image-to-image translation between two domains X and Y when
paired training examples are unavailable.
Describe the architecture of CycleGAN, including the two generators
G:X→Y, F:Y→X
and the two discriminators DY and DX. Explain how adversarial training is performed in both
directions.
Q8. Explain the concept of cycle consistency in CycleGAN. Derive and explain the complete
CycleGAN objective:
Explain the role of the cycle-consistency term, the parameter λ\lambda, and the two
adversarial losses. Why is cycle consistency important when training with unpaired images?

Variants of VAE
Q1. How does a Convolutional VAE address the curse of dimensionality? Illustrate the
architecture of a Convolutional VAE.
Q2. Explain the architecture and objective of a Conditional VAE (CVAE). How does
conditioning on labelled information influence the latent representation and generated output?
Q3. Explain the working principle of β-VAE. Derive/write its modified objective function and
explain the role of the hyperparameter β\beta in controlling the information capacity of the latent
channel. Discuss how β-VAE encourages disentangled representations.
Q4. Explain the motivation for Ladder VAE (LVAE). How does it learn a hierarchical latent
representation? Compare a conventional hierarchical VAE with the ladder architecture using a
suitable diagram.
Q5. A β-VAE has a reconstruction loss of 18.5 and a KL-divergence loss of 2.4 for a given
training sample.
The β-VAE objective is given by
Calculate the objective value for:
(a) β=1
(b) β=2
(c) β=4
Explain how increasing β changes the relative importance of the KL-divergence term and
discuss its effect on the information capacity of the latent representation.
Q6. A vanilla VAE uses a fully connected layer to transform an image representation of size
64×64×3 into a feature vector of size 512.
(a) Calculate the number of weights required in this fully connected layer, ignoring biases.
(b) Suppose the convolutional VAE first reduces the image to a feature representation of size
8×8×64 and then uses a fully connected layer to produce the same 512-dimensional
representation. Calculate the number of weights in this layer.
(c) Calculate the reduction in the number of weights and explain why convolutional architectures
are preferable for high-dimensional image inputs in VAEs.
